reasons: shell_guard.py's _resolution_walk treats `git -C <dir>` exactly like `cd <dir>`: it reassigns the shared `current` base directory for every *later* chain part, not only for the git invocation it belongs to (plugin/hooks/shell_guard.py, the `git_c is not None` branch sets `current = _resolve(current, dirarg2)` and then falls through to the same loop as `cd`). Real shells do not work this way: `git -C <dir> ...` changes the working directory only for that one git process, never for a sibling command joined by `;`/`&&`/`||`/`|` in the same line. So a command such as `git -C docs status && echo x > CLAUDE.md` actually writes to the project's real root CLAUDE.md (bash's own cwd is untouched by `git -C`), but the hook resolves the second part's `CLAUDE.md` against `docs/` because `current` was left pointing at `docs` by the first part. `protected_paths.ALWAYS_PROTECTED`'s `/CLAUDE.md` is root-anchored, so `docs/CLAUDE.md` is 'ordinary project content' (protected_paths.py's own docstring) and `_check_one` returns None: `decide()` returns `Decision.allow()` while the real write lands on the guardrail file. The same construction works with any already-allowed CI command containing a harmless `git -C <subdir> <read-only-verb>` ahead of the write, and needs no non-literal token, so the fail-closed rule for `$VAR`/`$()`/glob never fires either.

This is the exact class of vulnerability change 0002 exists to close (intent.md: 'an unattended phase session can overwrite CLAUDE.md, REVIEW.md, sdlc.yaml or .claude/** ... bypassing the guardrail-file protection'), reopened through a different vector inside the very hook meant to close it. Outside CI -- a by-hand run, native Windows, or any host with no sandbox -- spec.md's own Flagged concerns say the hook is the *only* layer ('a by-hand run on Windows, or on any host with no sandbox, has the hook alone'); on such a host this bypass is complete and silent, with no sandbox denyWrite and no hook denial, and nothing would be visible until (if ever) the gate's diff-based check_guardrails sees a committed guardrail change -- which a transient, reverted-before-commit write (the exact scenario intent.md names) never produces.

The gap is not the residual risk plan.md names and accepts: plan.md's Risks section accepts 'a command the idiom list does not recognise (an unlisted wrapper, content decoded and piped to an interpreter)' as a known, named residual outside CI. The git -C chain-persistence bug is a different thing -- a recognised idiom (plain redirection) on a recognised, explicitly-tested construct (`git -C`) whose chain-wide side effect was never reasoned about -- so it was not weighed and accepted, it was missed.

No test in the diff could catch this: test_shell_guard_resolves_a_git_dash_c_target only ever puts `git -C <dir> <verb> <path>` alone in the command, never followed by a second, unrelated chain part; every other case parametrized in test_shell_guard_allows_ordinary_commands / test_shell_guard_resolves_after_a_cd_in_the_same_chain chains only `cd` (which genuinely does persist in a real shell) with a write, never `git -C` with a later, independent write. The full suite as written would pass unchanged with this bug present.
classification_reasons: Spec is not tight even on its own terms: Flagged concerns accept a residual heuristic-parsing gap rather than eliminate it, closed only partially (CI only) by the sandbox layer, and the spec itself names the native-Windows/no-sandbox case as hook-alone.

Blast radius is wide: shell_guard.py runs on every Bash/PowerShell call in every phase, by hand and in CI; plugin/ci/settings.ci.json and plugin/ci/run_phase.py's ci_settings_file add a new sandbox.filesystem.denyWrite path read by every CI phase job; sdlc.yaml's risk_list item 'auth' is touched end to end; three pre-existing tests (test_ci.py, test_evals.py) have their contracts changed on purpose.

No pre-existing test exercised a Bash/PowerShell write to a guardrail or locked test file before this change -- the whole behavior is new, not already covered by current tests -- and, per the finding above, the new tests still leave a chain-based bypass through `git -C` unexercised.
attempted: Intent: the diff's shell_guard.py, hooks.json registration, and sandbox.filesystem.denyWrite block do target the finding in intent.md (Bash/PowerShell bypass of protected_paths.py/test_file_lock.py). The design is on-target in shape, but see Proof/Tests below for where its own mechanism reopens the same class of gap.

Spec and plan: files touched (shell_guard.py, hooks.json, settings.ci.json, run_phase.py, test_hooks.py, test_ci.py, test_evals.py, OPERATING_MODEL.md, plugin.json, marketplace.json) match plan.md's Files-that-change list exactly, with status.yaml/evidence bookkeeping as the only additions, which is expected for a phase-(c) commit. plan.md's Order of work steps 1-7 are all represented in the diff. Step 8 (paste pytest/ruff/compileall output) is not represented as literal evidence in this diff, but per the brief and verifier.md this is a CI session where the runner, not the writer, produces build/test/lint logs after the session -- not something I judge or cite against the change (REVIEW.md: evidence/** is out of scope for findings).

Proof: read plugin/hooks/shell_guard.py's full tokenizer and resolver logic line by line (not the author's description of it) and traced _resolution_walk's handling of `git -C` against real shell semantics; found that it mutates the shared `current` base directory for the rest of the chain exactly as `cd` does, which is wrong for `git -C` and produces a live authorization bypass (detailed in reasons). Compared this against every git-C-related test in the diff's tests/test_hooks.py and plan.md's Proof section; none chains `git -C` with a later, unrelated write.

Blast radius: confirmed the new hook runs on every Bash/PowerShell call everywhere (hooks.json diff), confirmed the sandbox.filesystem.denyWrite addition is CI-only per spec.md and plan.md (by design, not an oversight), and confirmed the three risk-named test-contract changes (test_ci.py's dropped `sandbox == source['sandbox']` equality, test_evals.py's FRAMEWORK_SUITE derivation) are each reasoned in plan.md's Risks as deliberate, not silent, weakenings.

Policies: security-baseline (reuse existing matching primitives rather than duplicating; no new dependency -- confirmed shell_guard.py imports only protected_paths/test_file_lock/_common/stdlib re/shlex-style hand-rolled parsing) and coding-standards rule 4 (no pre-existing test weakened without a reasoned contract change) both applied as documented; the real gap found is a logic defect in new code, not a skipped policy.

Tests: walked through whether the added tests could pass with a meaningful bug still present, per angle 6 -- they can: the git -C chain-persistence bug survives the full test suite as written, because no test combines a `git -C <dir>` part with a subsequent unrelated write in the same chain, which is exactly the shape needed to trigger it.
